XHDATA D-219 Review

An ultra-budget analog-dial DSP receiver — full video review, specs, and verdict below.

Specifications

BandsFM1 87–108 MHz, FM2 64–87 MHz, MW 520–1710 kHz (10K steps, US version) / 522–1620 kHz (9K steps), SW 4.75–22.0 MHz across 9 sub-bands
TuningAnalog dial (potentiometer-driven) over a Si4825-A10 DSP chip — not digital/PLL. Needle pointer, no display
Audio outputMono, to both the internal speaker and the 3.5mm headphone jack
Power2x AA batteries, or 5V/300mA DC external adapter (diode-protected so external power won’t damage installed batteries)
Antenna~20.5–21in (55cm) telescopic whip, rotates 360°
ExtrasWrist strap, rear kickstand, no dial light, no FM stereo, no SSB
Weight~150g without batteries
Typical price~$7–$8

Pros

  • Genuinely simple to use — three bands, one dial, no menus
  • Precise analog tuning with very little play in the wheel
  • Long telescopic antenna helps both FM and SW reception
  • Runs on 2 AA batteries; diode-protected DC input is a nice touch at this price

Cons

  • Mono output only — even through headphones
  • No SSB, no digital frequency readout, no memories
  • Some owners report a subset of units developing intermittent noise or going silent after limited use — worth a burn-in test after purchase
  • 9K vs 10K MW step version varies by region — confirm which you’re buying

Verdict

The D-219 is not built for serious DXing — it’s a mono, no-frills analog radio at a mono, no-frills analog price. What it does well: the tuning dial has real precision for something this cheap, band-switching is dead simple, and the telescopic antenna is generously long for the size of the unit. Independent reviewers (SWLing Post, Radio-Timetraveller) consistently describe it as punching above its price for casual listening, travel, or as a first radio — while flagging the same durability concerns we noted above. If you want a serious portable, look higher up our Equipment page. If you want a cheap, easy analog radio to keep in a bag or hand to a beginner, the D-219 does that job.

Specs verified against XHDATA’s official site, SWLing Post, and Radiomuseum.org; owner-reliability notes drawn from SWLing Post reader comments.
